title: Water & Sewer Line Construction in the US
one_liner: A mostly public-funded civil construction market tied to municipal water mains, sewer networks, treatment plants and aging-infrastructure mandates.
overview: This industry builds, reconstructs and repairs water mains, sewers, drains, aqueducts, pumping stations, treatment plants and storage tanks. The 2022 baseline showed a mature, fragmented industry with $53.7 billion of revenue, 16,103 enterprises, 162,635 employees and a 2022 profit margin of 3.6%. Demand is driven mainly by state and local government water and wastewater capital programs, with federal programs becoming more visible through 2022-2026 IIJA State Revolving Fund and WIFIA funding. Census construction-spending data show the adjacent water-supply and sewage/waste-disposal categories running at a combined 2025 average annualized rate of about $89.6 billion, up sharply from 2024, although contractor revenue recognition still lags project awards and appropriations.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated industry revenue of about $54.2 billion, based on the 2022 IBISWorld baseline and its 2022-2027 forecast path
key_stats.growth: 2025 estimated industry revenue growth of about 0.3%, based on the 2022-2027 IBISWorld forecast path
key_stats.adjacent_construction_spending: 2025 Census/FRED annualized average of about $36.2 billion for water supply construction and $53.4 billion for sewage and waste-disposal construction; 2026 first-half averages were about $35.7 billion and $53.5 billion, respectively

baseline_2022.growth: 2017-2022 revenue CAGR of 1.3%, with 2022 revenue growth estimated at 0.1%

how_it_makes_money: Contractors earn revenue by bidding on and delivering public and private projects for water mains, sewer lines, treatment plants, pumping stations, storage tanks, drains and related utility connections. The 2022 product mix was water mains and other water supply infrastructure at 33.7% of revenue, sewer lines and other sewer infrastructure at 29.2%, sewage and water treatment plants at 18.5%, building-related utility connections at 6.2%, highway-related drainage work at 1.7% and other construction at 10.7%. Larger contractors may act as prime contractors or construction managers, while many smaller firms perform excavation, pipe installation, rehabilitation and specialty trade work under municipal or utility contracts.
cost_structure: The 2022 baseline shows a low-margin industry, with profit at 3.6% of revenue and wages at about 22.6% of revenue. Major cost buckets are labor, pipe and fittings, concrete, steel, aggregates, equipment, fuel, subcontractors, bonding and insurance. Input pressure remains relevant in 2026: BLS/FRED data show plastics water pipe PPI at 183.22 in May 2026, down 10.84% from May 2025, while BLS concrete-pipe PPI averaged 397.857 in 2025 and was 399.708 in May 2026, indicating some easing in plastics but persistent pricing in concrete products.
major_players: Regional municipal utility contractors and specialty excavation firms
current_dynamics: Public funding remains the core demand source. EPA programs are channeling 2022-2026 IIJA money through Drinking Water SRF, Clean Water SRF, lead-service-line replacement and WIFIA loans, while local rate increases, bond issuance and state water funds determine how quickly projects reach contractors. Census/FRED data show water-supply construction spending averaged about $36.2 billion in 2025, up 7.7% from 2024, and sewage/waste-disposal construction averaged about $53.4 billion in 2025, up 14.3% from 2024. In 2026, the first-half annualized average was roughly flat at about $89.3 billion combined, suggesting a high backlog environment but slower sequential momentum.
whats_growing: Lead-service-line replacement, PFAS and emerging-contaminant treatment, water reuse, wastewater treatment upgrades, sewer conveyance repair, stormwater resilience and Sun Belt capacity expansions are growing. EPA’s 2022 Clean Watersheds Needs Survey, released in 2024 and maintained in 2026, identified $630.1 billion of 2022-2041 clean-water needs, including $151.1 billion for conveyance repair and new conveyance and $115.3 billion for stormwater management. EPA’s 2025 update to drinking-water needs identified $422.9 billion for distribution and transmission, directly supporting pipeline rehabilitation and replacement demand.
whats_shrinking: Lower-priority new extensions in slow-growth municipalities, purely speculative residential tie-in work and projects dependent on discretionary local borrowing are under pressure in 2025-2026. The 2026 first-half water-supply construction average of about $35.7 billion was about 1.2% below the 2025 average, showing some cooling after the 2024-2025 surge. Traditional lowest-bid design-bid-build work is also losing share to design-build and construction-manager-at-risk delivery, especially for complex treatment and conveyance projects.
recent_developments: 2024-10: EPA finalized Lead and Copper Rule Improvements requiring drinking-water systems to identify and replace lead pipes within 10 years.
2025-03: ASCE’s 2025 Report Card graded U.S. drinking water C-, wastewater D+ and stormwater D, reinforcing long-term replacement demand.
2025-05: EPA issued FY 2025 SRF allotments for IIJA and base drinking-water and clean-water programs.
2025-11: EPA announced $6.5 billion of new WIFIA funding plus $550 million for State WIFIA financing.
2025-11: EPA announced $3.0 billion in new SRF funding for lead reduction and $1.1 billion of redistributed unused DWSRF lead funding.
2026-05: Census/FRED reported May 2026 annualized construction spending of $35.8 billion for water supply and $53.5 billion for sewage and waste disposal.
outlook: The 2025-2030 outlook is steady rather than high-growth. The 2022 IBISWorld forecast pointed to only modest revenue expansion through 2027, and current data support that view: public capital programs are stronger, but industry revenue is constrained by municipal borrowing costs, labor availability, long procurement cycles and the lag between federal allotments and completed construction. The best-positioned contractors are those with municipal relationships, trenchless and rehabilitation capabilities, design-build experience, bonding capacity and exposure to lead, PFAS, reuse and resilience mandates.
themes: IIJA and State Revolving Fund funding

title: Web Design Services
one_liner: A fragmented market of agencies, freelancers and platform specialists building and maintaining websites as AI and no-code tools reshape demand.
overview: Web design services include website graphic design, UX and interface design, front-end and related code work, CMS implementation, SEO setup, redesigns and maintenance, excluding native app development and direct online retail operations. The 2022 baseline report framed the industry as a declining $11.0 billion market hurt by DIY builders and market saturation; current 2025 public IBIS/R&M pages show a much larger $47.4 billion revenue base with 2.3% CAGR over 2020-2025 and 203,000 businesses, indicating a revised or broader series that should not be compared mechanically with the older PDF. Demand in 2025-2026 is strongest where websites are tied to commerce, lead generation, speed, accessibility, mobile UX, analytics and AI-search visibility rather than one-off brochure builds.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: $47.4 billion US revenue, per public IBIS/R&M listing for Web Design Services in the US.
key_stats.growth: 2020-2025: 2.3% revenue CAGR; 2025 market projected to grow over 2025-2030, per public IBIS/R&M listing.
key_stats.businesses: 2025: 202,692-203,000 businesses; 2025 business-count growth 3.6%; 2020-2025 business-count CAGR 4.9%, per IBISWorld public statistics.
key_stats.employment: 2025: about 889,000 employees, per public IBIS/R&M listing.
key_stats.small_business_website_adoption: 2025: 83% of US small businesses had a website, up from 64% in 2018; 12% launched one in the prior year, per Clutch.
key_stats.ecommerce_driver: 2025: US retail e-commerce sales totaled $1.2337 trillion, up 5.4% from 2024 and equal to 16.4% of total retail sales, per Census/FRED-derived releases.
key_stats.cms_platform_context: 2026-07: WordPress used by 41.2% of all websites and 59.1% of CMS websites; Shopify 5.3% of all websites and 7.6% CMS share; Wix 4.3% and 6.1%; Squarespace 2.5% and 3.5%, per W3Techs.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: $11.004 billion revenue in 2022 dollars, per local IBISWorld baseline PDF.
baseline_2022.growth: 2017-2022: revenue fell at a 3.1% annualized rate; 2022 revenue expected to fall 1.9%, per local baseline.
baseline_2022.profit: 2022: $616 million profit and 5.6% profit margin, per local baseline.
baseline_2022.wages: 2022: $4.242 billion total wages, per local baseline.
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022: custom platform web development 54.9% of revenue, WordPress web development 32.5%, other content platform web development 12.6%, per local baseline.

how_it_makes_money: Project fees for custom website design, redesign and front-end development.
CMS implementation and customization for WordPress, Shopify, Squarespace, Wix, Webflow and other platforms.
Monthly retainers for maintenance, hosting coordination, security updates, analytics, CRO, accessibility fixes and content updates.
Bundled digital services including SEO setup, landing pages, performance optimization, conversion tracking and e-commerce enablement.
Specialized UX/UI, design-system and component work for larger clients that treat websites as continuously updated digital products.

cost_structure.labor: 2025: compensation is the largest cost; public IBIS/R&M summary says nearly half of revenue goes to specialized developers and engineers, though many low-revenue freelancers pull average wage metrics down.
cost_structure.profit: 2022: 5.6% margin in the baseline; 2025 public pages withhold the exact profit value but describe a fragmented market with cost and pricing pressure.
cost_structure.software_and_tools: Ongoing spending on design software, CMS plugins, hosting, testing, analytics, AI tools, stock assets, security tooling and collaboration platforms.
cost_structure.sales_and_marketing: Client acquisition through referrals, search, marketplaces, paid ads, proposal work and portfolio development is material because the market is highly fragmented.
cost_structure.overhead: Rent and utilities are low for freelancers and remote agencies; larger firms carry management, QA, project management and compliance overhead.
cost_structure.purchases_and_subcontractors: Agencies often subcontract copywriting, SEO, photography, animation, accessibility, back-end development and paid media work.

major_players: No company holds more than 5% share in the 2025 IBIS/R&M public listing.
Digital marketing and advertising agencies with web practices
current_dynamics: AI site builders are lowering entry-level build costs and compressing timelines, shifting professional demand toward brand differentiation, integrations, conversion, governance and ongoing optimization.
No-code and hosted commerce platforms are both competitors and channels: they reduce basic custom-build demand while creating paid implementation and customization work.
Small businesses continue to adopt websites, but many choose platform templates or owner-built sites before hiring agencies for redesign, SEO, e-commerce or performance fixes.
E-commerce growth supports Shopify, WooCommerce and custom checkout projects, while mobile UX and page-speed work remain recurring needs.
The market is extremely fragmented, with remote work and offshore talent keeping price competition high.
WordPress remains dominant, but its CMS share is slowly eroding as Shopify, Wix, Squarespace, Webflow and AI-native builders gain share.
whats_growing: AI-assisted website generation, copy, image, layout and redesign workflows.
Shopify and commerce-focused implementation, including storefront design, checkout optimization and product-content systems.
Maintenance retainers, security updates, accessibility remediation, analytics, speed optimization and conversion-rate optimization.
Mobile-first redesigns and lightweight performance work as websites compete for search, social and AI-referred traffic.
Small-business website launches and refreshes: 2025 Clutch data shows 90% of small businesses planned website investment over the next 12 months.
whats_shrinking: Simple brochure-site projects that can be handled by AI builders or templates.
Purely custom builds for price-sensitive small businesses where Wix, Squarespace, Shopify or WordPress templates are good enough.
Legacy CMS and older open-source platform work such as Joomla and Drupal for small clients, as W3Techs 2026 data shows lower share than WordPress and hosted builders.
One-time redesign projects without maintenance, SEO, analytics or conversion scope.
Low-differentiation freelance production work exposed to offshore competition and marketplace pricing.
recent_developments: 2025-03-05: Shopify released an AI store setup tool for Basic-plan-and-up merchants, generating custom store themes from a business description.
2025-08-21: Clutch reported 83% of US small businesses had a website, up from 64% in 2018, with DIY builders powering 41% of small-business sites.
2026-03-10: Census Q4 2025 release showed full-year 2025 US retail e-commerce sales of $1.2337 trillion, up 5.4% from 2024.
2026-05-05: Shopify reported Q1 2026 revenue growth of 34% and more than $100 billion in quarterly GMV, underscoring commerce-platform demand.
2026-07-27: W3Techs showed WordPress at 41.2% of all websites and Shopify/Wix continuing to hold the No. 2 and No. 3 CMS positions.
2026-08-05: Shopify’s Q2 2026 results, reported by financial media, showed about $3.58 billion in revenue and roughly 32% GMV growth, reinforcing platform-led e-commerce momentum.
outlook: Through 2026-2030, web design services should grow more slowly than the broader digital economy but remain resilient where providers attach design work to measurable business outcomes. Basic site creation will keep commoditizing as AI, templates and hosted builders improve; higher-value demand will concentrate in e-commerce, accessibility, mobile performance, conversion optimization, design systems, analytics, security and AI-search readiness. The best-positioned firms will sell websites as living revenue infrastructure rather than static creative projects.

title: Website Creation Software Developers
one_liner: US website creation software developers sell no-code, low-code and AI-assisted tools that help businesses and individuals build, host, manage and monetize websites.
overview: Website Creation Software Developers includes companies that develop and publish website design, editing, no-code, low-code and site-management software. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline defined the industry around HTML editing and website design software, with revenue of $12.781 billion in 2022 after 0.1% growth that year. Applying the baseline 2022-2028 projected CAGR of 2.45% implies broad US industry revenue of about $13.7 billion in 2025 and about $14.1 billion in 2026. Current demand is being reshaped by AI-assisted creation, hosted commerce, subscription bundles, domain and hosting integration, payment tools, SEO, analytics and app marketplaces. Public market estimates for the narrower global website-builder software segment vary widely, from $2.8 billion in 2025 to $4.9 billion in 2025 depending on scope, confirming that the IBIS industry is broader than drag-and-drop builders alone.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: approximately $13.7 billion US industry revenue, derived from the 2022 IBISWorld baseline of $12.781 billion and its 2022-2028 projected 2.45% CAGR
key_stats.growth: 2025: approximately 2.45% broad US industry growth, using the IBISWorld 2022-2028 projected CAGR
key_stats.market_size_2026: 2026: approximately $14.1 billion US industry revenue on the same projection basis
key_stats.profit_margin: 2022: 21.5% IBISWorld industry profit margin; profitability is expected to compress toward 19.7% by 2027 as wages and new entrants rise
key_stats.wages: 2022: $4.717 billion total wages in the IBISWorld baseline
key_stats.ecommerce_driver: 2025: US retail e-commerce sales were $1.234 trillion, up 5.4%, and represented 16.4% of total retail sales
key_stats.narrow_market_context: 2026: Mordor Intelligence valued the global website builders market at $3.57 billion; Custom Market Insights estimated global website builder software at $2.8 billion in 2025 and $2.9 billion in 2026

how_it_makes_money: Operators primarily earn recurring subscription revenue from website builder plans, hosted CMS tools, premium templates, AI creation tools, domain connection, ad-free publishing, storage, bandwidth, security, booking tools, e-commerce storefronts, payment processing, app-market commissions, email and productivity bundles, agency seats and enterprise collaboration plans. Freemium acquisition remains common: free site creation lowers adoption friction, while paid tiers monetize custom domains, commerce, analytics, SEO, automation, support and higher usage limits.
cost_structure: The largest operating costs are software engineering wages, cloud hosting and infrastructure, customer support, sales and marketing, payment and domain-related pass-through costs, product development, content/template creation, security and compliance. The 2022 baseline reported $4.717 billion in wages and warned that wages would rise faster than revenue, reaching a projected $5.8 billion by 2027. Public 2025 filings show the cost mix clearly: Wix reported 2025 Creative Subscriptions cost of revenue of $237.3 million, including higher revenue-related costs, hosting costs and domain costs; Shopify reported 2025 subscription solutions cost of revenue of $520 million; GoDaddy reported 2025 total cost of revenue of $1.8015 billion, or 36.4% of revenue.
major_players: Wix.com Ltd. - 2025 revenue of $1.99 billion, including $1.41 billion Creative Subscriptions revenue and 6.1 million premium subscriptions; central AI products include Wix Harmony, Aria, Astro and Base44
GoDaddy Inc. - 2025 total revenue of $4.951 billion and 2025 Applications and Commerce revenue of $1.889 billion, including proprietary website building and commerce products
Squarespace Inc. - taken private by Permira in 2024 in a transaction valued at about $7.2 billion; remains a major design-led website and commerce platform
Shopify Inc. - 2025 revenue of $11.556 billion, including $2.752 billion Subscription Solutions revenue; a key competitor where storefront creation is tied to commerce infrastructure
Webflow Inc. - private visual development and CMS platform; reported in 2026 that more than 60,000 websites had been published using its AI site builder
Block Inc./Weebly - Weebly remains part of Block's Square seller ecosystem, competing through bundled online store and payments functionality
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is shifting from template libraries toward AI-assisted workflows that generate site structure, copy, imagery, stores, compliance pages and backend logic from prompts. Demand remains strongest among small businesses, creators, agencies and commerce-led users that want a low-cost alternative to custom web development. E-commerce is still a key demand driver: US retail e-commerce reached $1.234 trillion in 2025 and increased its share of total retail sales to 16.4%. At the same time, the industry is more competitive because AI-native app builders, WordPress ecosystems, open-source tools, hosting companies and commerce platforms are converging on the same customer budget.
whats_growing: AI site generation, conversational editing, agentic website operations, mobile-first sites, integrated e-commerce, payment processing, booking tools, SEO automation, compliance-policy generation, analytics, performance hosting, agency workspaces and higher-value subscription tiers are growing in 2025-2026. Vendor results show this mix: Wix 2025 Business Solutions revenue rose 18%, GoDaddy 2025 Applications and Commerce revenue rose 14.3%, and Shopify 2025 Subscription Solutions revenue rose to $2.752 billion.
whats_shrinking: Standalone HTML editors, one-time license sales, desktop-only website design tools, purely static brochure-site builders, ad-supported free tiers, low-value premium subscriptions and unsupported legacy products continue to lose relevance. Adobe Muse support ended in 2020, and the baseline already identified mature design software as exposed to slower growth. In 2025, Wix reported premium subscriptions declined 1% to 6.1 million as it prioritized higher-value users over raw subscriber additions.
recent_developments: 2025-04-09: Wix launched Astro, an AI-powered assistant for site and business management in the Wix dashboard.
2025-09-17: Webflow announced broader Webflow AI updates, including agentic workflows, MCP capabilities, AI optimization suggestions and AI-powered SEO.
2025-11-13: GoDaddy launched Airo.ai in beta, an agentic AI experience that can register domains, build Website Builder sites, generate logos and draft policy templates from a conversation.
2026-01-21: Wix announced Wix Harmony, a flagship AI website builder combining Aria, vibe-coding style creation and drag-and-drop visual control.
2026-02-05: Webflow expanded its AI site builder to support multi-page site creation, structure, styles and animations, with Enterprise access.
2026-05-11: GoDaddy launched Airo for WordPress, bringing AI site creation, editing and WooCommerce setup into the WordPress workflow.
outlook: The US industry outlook through 2026 is positive but more competitive than the 2022 baseline. Broad industry revenue is estimated at about $14.1 billion in 2026 on the IBIS projection path, while narrower public website-builder market reports point to mid- to high-single-digit global growth depending on market definition. Growth should come from AI-assisted site creation, SMB e-commerce, premium commerce add-ons, agency workflows and bundled domain-hosting-commerce suites. Margin pressure will come from AI compute costs, cloud hosting, customer acquisition, engineering wages and the need to keep shipping features against AI-native rivals. The strongest platforms will be those that turn website creation into a broader operating system for selling, marketing, compliance, analytics and customer engagement.
themes: Competition from open-source and AI-native tools

title: Weight Loss Services in the US
one_liner: Traditional diet programs are being remade by GLP-1 drugs, telehealth, digital coaching and meal-delivery bundles.
overview: In 2022, the IBISWorld baseline described a mature, saturated industry built around commercial diet programs, in-person consultations, digital subscriptions, meal plans and product sales, with revenue of $3.787 billion and slow 2017-2022 growth. By 2025-2026, the market is structurally different: obesity prevalence remains high, digital access is normal, and GLP-1 medications have become the central competitive force. Legacy operators such as WeightWatchers and Medifast are trying to reposition around clinical care, medication support and higher-protein nutrition products, while meal-plan brands such as Jenny Craig have moved further online after bankruptcy and relaunch. The result is a bifurcated industry: traditional behavioral and meal-replacement programs are shrinking, but clinical, telehealth-enabled and GLP-1 companion services are growing.

key_stats.market_size: 2026: $2.3 billion-$2.7 billion in US commercial weight loss services revenue in the public Open Markets/IBISWorld concentration snapshot; broader US weight loss services estimates place the 2025 market at $10.3 billion when fitness, surgical and adjacent services are included.
key_stats.growth: 2025: legacy operators declined sharply, with WeightWatchers 2025 revenue down 9.6% year over year to $710.6 million and Medifast 2024 revenue down 43.8% year over year to $602.5 million; broader weight loss services forecasts point to 2025-2030 CAGR of about 7.6% as clinical and digital models expand.
key_stats.obesity_prevalence: 2021-August 2023: 40.3% of US adults age 20+ had obesity and 9.7% had severe obesity on an age-adjusted NHANES basis.
key_stats.state_obesity: 2024: all US states and territories had adult obesity prevalence of at least 25%, and Mississippi, West Virginia and Guam were at or above 40% in CDC BRFSS maps.
key_stats.weightwatchers: 2025: WeightWatchers reported $710.6 million total revenue, 2.761 million end-of-period subscribers and 130,000 clinical subscribers.
key_stats.medifast: 2024: Medifast reported $602.5 million revenue, 27,100 active earning OPTAVIA coaches and $2.1 million net income.

baseline_2022.growth: 2017-2022: 0.3% annualized revenue growth; 2022 revenue growth was estimated at 2.9%.
baseline_2022.forecast: 2022-2027 baseline forecast: 0.3% annualized revenue growth to about $3.9 billion.

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn revenue from digital subscriptions, in-person or virtual coaching fees, clinical weight-management subscriptions, employer and payer programs, branded prepared meals, meal replacements, supplements, app-based behavior-change tools, franchise fees and recurring product shipments. In 2025-2026, the fastest monetization is coming from higher-ARPU clinical memberships, GLP-1 companion programs, medication access workflows and nutrition support for people taking or tapering off obesity drugs.
cost_structure: Major costs include coach and clinician labor, food and supplement sourcing, fulfillment and shipping, marketing/customer acquisition, app and telehealth platform development, payment processing, rent for remaining physical sites, franchise support, insurance and compliance. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline showed a relatively labor-light but marketing-intensive model with 2022 wages of $808 million and 2022 profit margin of 8.8%; by 2025, clinical programs increased compliance and provider costs while digital delivery reduced dependence on physical locations.
major_players: LillyDirect and other pharma-linked access channels
current_dynamics: GLP-1 medications are both a substitute and a funnel. Consumers who once joined diet programs are increasingly seeking prescriptions, but many still need coaching, nutrition, muscle-preservation support and maintenance plans. WeightWatchers’ 2025 clinical revenue grew 44.7% even as total revenue fell 9.6%, showing the mix shift. Medifast’s 2024 revenue fell 43.8%, but the company launched GLP-1 nutrition support plans and reported that over 40% of active coaches were supporting at least one GLP-1 client by Q4 2024. Jenny Craig is operating as a virtual, meal-delivery-led brand after its 2023 bankruptcy and 2024 relaunch under Wellful. Noom, Ro, Hims & Hers and similar platforms are intensifying competition with telehealth, coaching and cash-pay medication programs.
whats_growing: Clinical weight management, GLP-1 access and companion programs, virtual coaching, employer and payer channels, high-protein and fiber-rich meal replacements, muscle-retention positioning, maintenance programs for patients stopping medication, app engagement tools, cash-pay subscription bundles and direct-to-consumer pharmacy partnerships.
whats_shrinking: Standalone in-person diet centers, workshop-heavy subscription models, non-clinical behavioral programs without medication integration, legacy packaged-food-only plans, small independent operators lacking digital acquisition capabilities and expensive programs that compete directly against lower-friction telehealth options.
recent_developments: 2024-02-27: Jenny Craig was reviewed as relaunched under Wellful with a fully online model and no physical weight loss centers.
2024-09-12: Noom announced a $129 compounded GLP-1 offering with a taper-off guarantee and GLP-1 companion positioning.
2024-12: Medifast launched OPTAVIA ASCEND, a high-protein, fiber-rich nutrition line for GLP-1 users and weight-management customers.
2025-01-08: GNC and Jenny Craig launched GNC Total Lean by Jenny Craig, pairing Jenny Craig meals with GNC shakes and snacks.
2025-06-17: WeightWatchers’ reorganization plan was confirmed, reducing debt by about $1.15 billion and shifting focus to integrated behavioral and clinical weight management.
2026-03-16: WeightWatchers reported 2025 revenue of $710.6 million, down 9.6%, while 2025 clinical subscription revenue rose 44.7% to $112.8 million.
outlook: Through 2026-2030, traditional commercial weight loss services are likely to remain pressured by GLP-1 adoption, low-cost apps and changing consumer expectations. Growth should come from hybrid models that combine medical access, behavioral support, nutrition, maintenance and employer distribution. Operators without clinical partnerships or strong digital acquisition will likely lose share, while brands with trusted communities, lower churn, provider networks and medication-adjacent services can grow even if legacy diet subscriptions decline.

title: Wheat, Barley & Sorghum Farming in the US
one_liner: A volatile grain-farming industry where 2025 farm receipts fell as lower wheat and barley prices offset resilient staple-food demand and stronger 2025/26 sorghum production.
overview: This industry covers farms growing wheat, barley, grain sorghum and related small grains where no single crop dominates the farm's total value of production. Wheat is the revenue anchor because it feeds flour milling, bread, pasta, cereal and export channels, while sorghum is tied to feed, food, beverage and biofuel demand and barley is tied heavily to malt, food, alcohol and industrial use. The industry is mature, fragmented and price-driven: revenue can change quickly with global wheat prices, drought, yields, the US dollar and grain export demand. Using USDA NASS value-of-production data as the current farm-receipts proxy, 2025 market size was $12.12 billion across wheat, barley and grain sorghum, compared with $13.22 billion in 2024.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: $12.12 billion value of production for wheat, barley and grain sorghum combined
key_stats.production: 2025/26: wheat 54.010 million metric tons, barley 3.067 million metric tons and sorghum 11.096 million metric tons

baseline_2022.exports: 2022: $10.3 billion, equal to 65.6% of industry revenue

how_it_makes_money: Farms earn revenue by selling harvested wheat, barley and sorghum to grain elevators, wholesalers, millers, maltsters, animal-feed manufacturers, food manufacturers, exporters and biofuel channels. Prices are generally set by commodity markets, crop quality, local basis, storage timing and contract terms rather than by farm-level branding. Government programs and crop insurance can supplement income in low-price or weather-disrupted years.
cost_structure: Major costs include seed, fertilizer, chemicals, fuel, repairs, irrigation or water, custom operations, equipment ownership, land rent, taxes, insurance, interest and hired or unpaid labor. USDA ERS reported that fertilizer represented 34% to 45% of wheat operating costs during 2020-2025, making nitrogen and other fertilizer prices a key margin driver. Machinery, land and working-capital costs keep capital intensity high, while family labor and owner-operated farms keep paid-wage shares lower than in many industries.
major_players: No major national company: 2025 industry structure remained highly fragmented across family farms, partnerships and owner-operators
Regional grain cooperatives and elevators are important marketing counterparties but generally operate as buyers or intermediaries rather than crop-farm producers
Large farms in Kansas, North Dakota, Montana, Texas, Oklahoma, Washington and Idaho influence supply locally, but no individual producer has material national share
current_dynamics: The 2025 farm-receipts picture weakened because prices fell across all three core crops: wheat averaged $4.90 per bushel in 2025, barley $5.40 per bushel in 2025 and grain sorghum $6.45 per cwt in 2025. Wheat remained the largest revenue source at $9.85 billion in 2025, but USDA ERS flagged a tougher 2026/27 wheat balance sheet with production forecast down 23% year over year and ending stocks forecast down 21% to 722 million bushels. Sorghum is the bright spot on volume, with USDA FAS showing 2025/26 production up 27% from 2024/25 to 11.096 million metric tons. Barley is pressured by lower beer production and weaker malt demand, with ERS forecasting 2024/25 barley food, alcohol and industrial use at 110.7 million bushels, down 27% from 2016/17.
whats_growing: 2025/26 sorghum production: 11.096 million metric tons, up 27% from 2024/25
2026/27 feed-grain production: USDA ERS July 2026 forecast of 420.1 million metric tons, with sorghum accounting for most of the June-to-July increase
2026/27 wheat scarcity: USDA ERS July 2026 forecast ending stocks down 21% to 722 million bushels, supporting price sensitivity if demand holds
2025/26 wheat role in field crops: USDA ERS reported wheat remained third among US field crops by planted acreage, production and gross farm receipts
whats_shrinking: 2025 combined farm receipts: $12.12 billion, down 8.3% from 2024
2025 wheat value of production: $9.85 billion, down 9.8% from 2024
2025 barley value of production: $0.73 billion, down 15.3% from 2024
2026/27 wheat production: USDA ERS July 2026 forecast down 23% year over year
2024/25 barley food, alcohol and industrial use: forecast at 110.7 million bushels, down 27% from 2016/17
recent_developments: 2025-07-23: USDA ERS reported barley food, alcohol and industrial use for 2024/25 at a forecast all-time low of 110.7 million bushels.
2026-02-26: USDA NASS reported 2025 wheat, barley and grain sorghum value of production at a combined $12.12 billion.
2026-04-08: USDA ERS reported 2025/26 US wheat production at about 2.0 billion bushels from 37.2 million harvested acres.
2026-07-15: USDA ERS forecast 2026/27 US wheat production down 23% year over year and ending stocks down 21% to 722 million bushels.
2026-07-15: USDA ERS raised 2026/27 US feed-grain production to 420.1 million metric tons and said sorghum drove most of the monthly increase.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is mixed. Lower 2025 prices reset revenue below the 2022 IBIS peak, but tighter 2026/27 wheat supplies could stabilize or lift prices if exports and food use hold. Sorghum benefits from stronger 2025/26 production and feed/export channels, while barley faces structural pressure from declining beer production and weaker malt demand. Margins should remain volatile because fertilizer, fuel, interest rates, drought risk and basis levels can move faster than growers can adjust acreage. Over the medium term, larger and better-capitalized farms should be better positioned to absorb yield risk, buy precision equipment and manage storage or contract timing.
